rv.q: You can’t help thinking that on some profound level these two were made to be together.
Skylight is a keeper and this revival is one for the ages.
Daldry has drawn three exquisite performances from his cast, and they lock together both in sharp contrast and in melancholy harmony with one another.
The American transfer — which also includes Matthew Beard, reprising a terrific performance as Tom’s son, Edward — retains every scintilla of the production’s special spark.
It’s a fitting theatrical device because this show, quite simply, cooks.
Whatever the takeaway for audiences hankering for a good political brawl, it’s the tragic clash of human emotions that really stings.
For such a rich entertainment — laughs, tears, flying cutlery, and all
This Skylight still manages to suggest how right these two are for each other and how wrong, how much we want them to be together again even as we know they can’t.

Skylight, while it doesn’t burst with topical references, is very much a post-Thatcher, pre-Blair play, with capitalist bullyboys like Tom maintaining business as usual and disenchanted insiders like Kyra dedicating themselves to repairing the damage of the ’80s.
The lack of sexual chemistry between them makes you wonder why Kyra bothers to put up with Tom.
Unless you’re a fan of hers, don’t bother.
It picks you up and hurls you along for two hours, and then resolves with such dramatic rightness that you walk out completely satisfied and at the same time all shook up.
Under the expert guidance of director Stephen Daldry and its luminous, impassioned stars, the production becomes–to get back to the food–nothing short of a five-star meal.

"There is nothing quite like great acting to re-kindle one’s love affair with the theatre. That’s most certainly the case with “Skylight,” which has the added pleasure of playwright David Hare’s heart-rending eloquence. When a show is loaded with this much talent, it does not take much to captivate...
Whether Kyra and Tom can reconcile or not, this Skylight assures us, both will endure — as will the troubled, contradictory world around them.
This is a smashingly good production of what might be David Hare's finest play, with two of the season's most striking performances from Bill Nighy and Carey Mulligan.
Mulligan gives an engrossing performance, with a luminous charisma that gives way to defensive fury and childlike vulnerability.

A young woman and an older man whose affair ended in a white-hot flash attempt to reconnect in David Hare’s “Skylight,” an artfully performed drama set in the 1990s in Great Britain. It’s just opened at the Golden Theatre, with its cast intact from a West End run last year.
Under the direction of Stephen Daldry, the “Skylight” revival is best avoided if you’re a conservative.
Daldry and his company make the play into a believable and heartbreaking night spent with real people.
The heart, meanwhile, is all but bypassed.
Hare has fashioned a work that's as much about the economic and social divisions that define modern Britain as it is about the romantic entanglements of its central characters.
While sure to delight Anglophiles and political progressives alike, its popularity may baffle anyone with a serious interest in good stagecraft.
Seeing this many gifted artists come together is rare, and the results are divine.

Hare’s dialogue is smoothly written, yet his play makes for a rather talky, at times tedious two hours or so as Tom and Kyra alternate between rueful recollections of their relationship and sporadic explosions over their present states of mind.

cn.t: Mulligan and Nighy deliver astonishing performances in this Hare revival, though critics split on whether the 1995 play's political debates still resonate. Most praise the crackling chemistry and emotional intensity, but some find the drama talky and dated.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
